title: Is the Door Really Open?
text:
Many managers say their door is always open. In a study published in 2007, James Detert and Ethan Burris tested what really makes employees speak up with ideas and concerns. They collected surveys from more than three thousand employees and over two hundred managers in a large American restaurant chain, and asked managers to rate how often each of their staff offered suggestions to improve things.

The researchers compared two kinds of leader behavior. One was transformational leadership, a broad style that includes inspiring people, setting an example and paying attention to their development. The other was much narrower: managerial openness, meaning whether the manager listened, showed interest in new ideas and was willing to act on them.

Both were linked to more speaking up, but openness was the more consistent predictor. Its effect worked through what the authors called psychological safety: employees believed that speaking up would not be held against them. The link was strongest for the best performing employees, the very people whose ideas a manager most needs, who would otherwise have the most to lose by speaking up.
lesson: Saying your door is open is not enough. Show by how you react that ideas and bad news are welcome, especially to your strongest people.
source: Detert, J. R., and Burris, E. R. (2007). Leadership behavior and employee voice: Is the door really open? Academy of Management Journal, 50(4), 869-884.
